title: Pumpkin Greens
author: Maama Nakato
desc: Pumpkin leaves stripped of their hairy outer layer, soaked ten minutes in salted water with a little baking soda, then cooked down with garlic, onion, tomato and green pepper.
longDesc: Pumpkin leaves are eaten across Uganda and cooked differently depending on where you are from — stewed with groundnuts in some regions, lightly sautéed in others. The preparation is the part nobody tells you about: each leaf and stalk carries a thin hairy outer layer that has to be peeled off, and there is no good English word for it. After that a soak in salted water with baking soda draws out impurities and lets the sand settle. Then it is a straightforward pan of greens.
ingredients: 3 to 4 handfuls of pumpkin greens, chopped
steps: Peel the thin hairy outer layer off each leaf stalk, then thinly slice the greens.
Put water in a large bowl with the 2 tsp of salt and the 1 tsp of baking soda.
Add the greens and let them sit for about 10 minutes.
Wash the greens thoroughly and drain them completely.
Put a clean pan on high heat, add the oil and let it get hot.
Add the garlic and onions and cook for about 2 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and green pepper and stir well.
Let the tomatoes cook until tender, about 3 to 5 minutes, then mash them with the wooden spoon.
Add the pumpkin greens, mix well, and cook 5 to 10 minutes until tender.
chefTips: Peel the hairy layer off. It is fiddly and it is what makes the greens soft rather than scratchy, and there is no way round it.
Salt and baking soda in the soaking water draws out impurities, and letting the greens stand lets the sand settle to the bottom.
Use soft, tender leaves. Older ones stay tough however long you cook them.
Mash the tomatoes in the pan once they are tender. It gives you a sauce rather than pieces.
Drain them completely after washing. Wet greens water the pan down.
Cooked with groundnut paste instead of this treatment they become a stew rather than a side, and that is the other standard regional way of doing them.
Five to ten minutes is the range and tenderness is the cue.
commonMistakes: Missing the soak, so the dish is gritty.
Adding the greens before the tomatoes have broken down.
sources: Adapted from Sophia Musoki, 'How to Make Pumpkin Greens', A Kitchen In Uganda (1 November 2020) — all quantities, the peeling of the hairy outer layer, the salt-and-baking-soda soak, the sand-settling note and the mash-the-tomatoes step are hers.
Her observation that pumpkin greens are cooked in various forms depending on region, and are good in a groundnut stew as well as lightly sautéed, is from that post.
healthBenefits: Pumpkin leaves are high in iron, calcium, vitamin A and vitamin C.
A genuinely under-used green — more nutrient-dense than most cultivated leaves.
Entirely plant-based with a modest amount of oil.
culturalNote: Growing pumpkins for the leaves as much as the fruit is a habit Uganda shares across the region, and it is a good example of a plant being used whole — leaves as a green, young fruit cooked with beans, seeds roasted as a snack. The technique of peeling the hairy layer is the kind of knowledge passed on in a kitchen rather than in writing.
keywords: pumpkin leaves with tomato and garlic
